# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

_No cycle currently in progress._

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber.
The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
number. Long-tail entries
live in [todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the
[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Drop overhead adjustment; grade the run from raw batches —
   the 0.23.0 cycle, decided in
   [Replanning II](notes/chores/chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run)
   - remove startup calibration, the constants block, adjusted
     columns, and the `calibrate` command; raw values only,
     one README sentence on apparatus framing
   - `pick_inner` sizing from a ~1 ms micro-probe (low
     quantile over back-to-back timer pairs), never printed
   - per-run quality gauge computed at the end from the run's
     own data: samples land in raw time-ordered batches,
     per-batch summaries (floor, mean, census counts) feed the
     gauge, then bulk-record into the histogram; relocate the
     -5 grade machinery (signals, thresholds, letter, warnings)
   - absorbs the interference-crossover entry's rate analysis
     (below) — batches give it the time axis
   - the overhead.rs deletion largely replaces the planned
     acquisition/estimation refactor
2. Guard `--pin` pools smaller than the bench's thread
   placements, and deadline the estimate phase — `zcr-mpsc-2t
   --pin 8` put both spinning software threads on one logical
   CPU and appeared hung until ^C (2026-07-26, bug #1 in
   [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md#bugs))
   - track `core_for` requests in `RunCfg` (max `thread_idx`
     asked for); refuse the run when placements exceed unique
     CPUs in the pool — placement only goes through `core_for`
     when pinning is active, so the guard covers every path,
     and no pinning means the scheduler separates the spinners
     itself

1180	### Replanning II: drop the adjustment, grade the run
1181	
1182	Recorded 2026-07-26, after -5's first cross-machine outing.
1183	Three findings converged into a philosophy change: the
1184	remaining rungs (-6 warmup-until-stable, -7 report only what
1185	is applied) are retired, the cycle closes after -5, and the
1186	redesign is the "Drop overhead adjustment" Todo (the next
1187	cycle).
1188	
1189	**The r5-7600x F.** A demonstrably quiet r5-7600x graded F
1190	while the visibly busy 3900X got D. The self-checks read the
1191	mechanism correctly — drift bracket `l_start` 42.750 ->
1192	`l_end` 38.051 ns/sample, 11% *faster* (interference only
1193	slows; getting faster is a clock ramp); the ladder's per-iter
1194	falls monotonically 0.4275 -> 0.3680; the 12.7% slope cross
1195	and 12.5% repeat are the same event seen twice; meanwhile
1196	disturbed 0.07% and `frame/sample` 8.310 ns, dead on that
1197	box's documented 8.2±0.06. The cause was ours: `CAL_WARMUP`
1198	is ~40 us of spin against frequency-governor timescales of

Reacquainted — 0.22.0 published yesterday; two uncommitted notes edits (chores-04 `Commits:` backfill, cycle-protocol lesson on the empty-commit push mishap); no cycle in progress; Todo #1 is the 0.23.0 raw-batches redesign.

On the Criterion question: web-claude's description is accurate. Criterion's linear sampling mode times the closure at iteration counts `d, 2d, 3d, … Nd`, then fits OLS on the (iterations, elapsed) pairs and reports the slope. And notably, we already ran this exact experiment ourselves — the 0.22.0-4 rung ("slope from multi-N loop-only passes") *is* this technique, so we have direct evidence on how it behaves under our noise.

What the regression actually buys:

- The **intercept absorbs fixed per-sample overhead** — the timer reads and sample setup that happen once per sample regardless of N. That's the quantity our `frame/sample` calibration chased, and the regression removes it without a separate calibration phase or any subtraction, because it's estimated on the same data it's applied to. No transferability problem — this is the genuinely sound part, and it's why Criterion can report sub-nanosecond operations at all, where per-sample framing would otherwise dominate.
- The **slope still contains per-iteration overhead** (loop counter, the call into the closure, `black_box`). Criterion doesn't remove that any more than our raw numbers do. So it removes less than people usually assume.

Is it worth it under high noise? Mostly no, and for a structural reason: the regression sorts noise by whether it scales with N. Fixed per-sample noise lands harmlessly in the intercept — but the noise that actually hurt us is **time-proportional and one-sided** (preemption probability grows with elapsed time, interference only ever adds). That noise scales with N, so it lands directly in the slope, and OLS gives the largest-N samples — the longest ones, most likely to catch a preemption — the most leverage. So the regression defends against the component that cancels in A/B comparison anyway, and is defenseless against the component that doesn't. Our own -4/-5 data showed the outcome: the slope repeated precisely within a run but swung ~10% between runs with frequency regime — precision without accuracy, which is what drove Replanning II. (Criterion partially compensates with big sample counts, bootstrap CIs, and reporting median/MAD alongside the slope — but the headline number is still the OLS slope.)

So the verdict splits by purpose. For Criterion's purpose — one-shot absolute timing of arbitrary closures, including sub-ns ones, on machines it can't characterize — the regression is a reasonable engineering trade and better than a calibrate-then-subtract design (which we proved fragile). For this project's purpose — A/B on one harness, where the fixed framing is common-mode — it buys nothing the raw numbers don't already have, and the batch-pipeline gauge in Todo #1 addresses the time-proportional noise that regression structurally cannot.

The plain version: Criterion's trick automatically cancels the fixed cost of starting and stopping the stopwatch, which is clever and works. But the noise that plagued us isn't stopwatch cost — it's the machine randomly slowing down mid-measurement, and that gets baked into Criterion's answer just like it gets baked into ours. Since we only compare runs against each other on the same rig, the stopwatch cost cancels for free anyway, so the trick solves a problem we don't have and skips the one we do.

content.text:
The bug claim checks out, and verifying it surfaced something bigger that corrects my previous answer. Three things:

**The R² bug is real.** In `src/stats/bivariate/regression.rs`, on both master and the 0.5.1 release, the loop reads `ss_tot = ss_res + (y - y_bar).powi(2)` — assignment onto the current `ss_res`, not accumulation onto `ss_tot`. The final `ss_tot` is just the last iteration's residual sum plus one squared deviation, so the reported R² is meaningless. Web-claude is also right that the slope is unaffected (it's computed separately in `fit`). Conclusion: don't lean on Criterion's goodness-of-fit output.

**Criterion's regression has no intercept — I was wrong about that last turn.** The same file shows `Slope::fit` computes `xy / x2`: a through-origin fit, `y = m·x`. So my claim that "the intercept absorbs fixed per-sample overhead" was wrong — there is no intercept, and Criterion does *not* remove per-sample framing at all; it gets folded into the slope (small at large N, but a real upward bias). That makes web-claude's phrasing exactly right: an intercept fit would put you *ahead of* Criterion, not equal to it. It also weakens the case I made for Criterion's technique — the one genuinely sound thing I credited it with, it doesn't actually do.

**On the recommendation itself, I'd still let Replanning II stand.** The in-run intercept fit does fix the objection it targets — estimating overhead on the same data it's applied to kills the transferability problem, which is real progress over our startup calibration. But it answers only one of Replanning II's four objections. The others are untouched: additivity is itself an approximation on a superscalar CPU; the correction is ~1.5 ns with uncertainty a good fraction of itself; and for A/B on one harness the framing is common-mode and cancels unsubtracted. And the noise structure from last turn still applies — one-sided, time-proportional contamination lands in the *slope*, and because OLS with an intercept estimates slope and intercept jointly, a few contaminated high-N samples move both. That last point undercuts the canary idea specifically: intercept instability would confound frequency-regime shifts with ordinary interference, whereas the batch pipeline's floor-over-time series gives the same boost/thermal signal cleanly, with time resolution, and it's already the 0.23.0 design. There's also a mechanical cost the advice glosses over: an in-run regression needs multiple iteration counts per run, which cuts against the fixed `pick_inner` sizing and complicates the histogram (samples at different N have different variance and quantization).

So: adopt the skepticism about Criterion's R², enjoy the confirmation that an intercept fit would out-do Criterion, but I wouldn't reopen the drop decision. If the intercept-fit-as-instrument idea seems worth keeping, it fits naturally as a `## Ideas` entry ("revisitable, nothing forecloses it" — the config-file opt-in note in Replanning II already holds the door open); say the word and I'll add it.

The plain version: the bug is genuinely there — Criterion's "how well does the line fit" number is computed wrong, though its main timing number is fine. I also discovered Criterion's line is forced through zero, so it never separates out the fixed measurement cost — meaning the fancier version web-claude proposes really would be better than Criterion. But better than Criterion isn't the bar; our plan already sidesteps the whole problem by comparing raw numbers on the same rig, and the redesign we have queued watches for the machine warming up or slowing down more directly than the proposed canary would.

Fit a line to batch floor vs. time and the slope *is* the drift measurement — the drift-bracket signal from -5, but as a proper fit over the whole run instead of two endpoints, with residuals localizing bursts ("interference clustered at ~3.2 s") and a correctly-computed R² as a stability figure. It also answers the canary desire from web-claude's advice with a cleaner instrument — floor-vs-time slope tracks boost/thermal state directly, with time resolution, no intercept confound. One refinement given our one-sided noise: fit the *floors* (or use a robust estimator like Theil–Sen) rather than OLS on means, so bursts show up in residuals and census counts instead of dragging the trend line.

The plain version: yes to borrowing the fit-a-line trick, but point it at a different axis. Good instinct — and it's worth noticing that this proposal is very close to machinery we already built: the 0.22.0-4/-5 "multi-N loop-only passes" plus the `l_start`/`l_end` drift bracket *are* an N-sweep bracket at the run's edges. Replanning II retired them as *calibration* (produce a constant, subtract it). What you're proposing is keeping them as *instrumentation* (produce a QC signal, report it) — and that reframing dodges most of what killed them. So: yes, useful, under specific design constraints.

What the brackets add that the time regression can't:

- **Decomposition.** With fixed inner N, a batch-floor shift on the time axis is ambiguous — per-sample frame change or per-iteration change, you can't tell; with inner > 1 the frame is amortized and nearly invisible in the samples. An N-sweep gives slope and intercept separately, so start-vs-end comparison says *which* moved. Frequency ramps move per-iteration time; a frame shift with a stable slope points at something else. That's a diagnostic dimension the time axis simply doesn't have.
- **Coverage for short runs.** Exactly your case: a short run yields few batches, so the floor-vs-time fit is underpowered right when ramp contamination is most likely. The brackets don't shrink with run length.
- **The ramp detector.** The r5-7600x F taught us that a startup probe on a deep-idle box measures the ramp itself. As a *grade of the machine* that was wrong; as a start-vs-end disagreement flag it's precisely right — "this run began in a different frequency regime than it ended" is the single most useful warning a short run can carry.

The design constraints that keep it from re-becoming calibration:

- **Differential only.** Compare start bracket to end bracket, and run to run — never use either as an absolute number, never subtract anything. Differential use also cancels the model error we measured: the 3900X's ~9% ladder bend sits in both brackets of the same run, so it mostly drops out of the comparison. Absolute use is where the 10% regime swing bit us; differential use is robust to it.
- **Robust per-N points.** Floor (or low quantile) per N step, not means — the 0.22 pairing-discipline lesson, since one preemption in a ~ms bracket would otherwise fake a regime shift.
- **Outside the measured run.** Brackets don't touch acquisition: `pick_inner`'s fixed sizing stays, the histogram never sees bracket samples. This preserves my prior objection's target — it was varying N *within* the run that was bad.
- **Tiny output surface.** Two or three gauge signals (bracket slope shift %, intercept shift %, maybe per-bracket fit residual) feeding the letter grade — not a constants block. The scope-creep risk here is real; the moment a bracket number gets printed as "overhead," we're back where Replanning II started.

Alongside the time regression the roles split cleanly: batch-floor-vs-time watches the run's interior (drift trend, burst localization); the brackets watch the edges and decompose what the interior fit can only detect. The end bracket is the more trustworthy of the two (machine warm); the start bracket's job is mostly to disagree with it when the run started cold.

If they disagree, the machine changed speed during the run, which is exactly when a short run's numbers deserve a warning label. It complements the trend line we fit through the run itself: the trend line watches the middle, the self-tests guard the two ends, and neither one ever adjusts the reported numbers — they only grade them.

A count-based warmup's wall-clock duration scales with step cost: a ~1 ns bench gets ~10 µs of warmup, a ~1 µs bench gets ~10 ms. Frequency-governor ramps live at tens-to-hundreds of ms — the r5-7600x diagnosis. So the fastest benches, where per-sample numbers are most ramp-sensitive, get the *least* warmup in the only unit that matters to the governor, and `pick_inner`'s sizing probe runs mid-ramp on exactly those benches. The right shape is the retired -6 design, warm-until-stable: probe repeatedly until consecutive readings agree, with a hard cap. Replanning II mooted it *as calibration warmup* — but the run-warmup problem it solved never went away, and your question is the correct place for it to resurface. What makes it especially attractive now is that it fuses with the bracket idea from last turn:

- Warm by running short floor probes (or mini N-sweeps) back to back; terminate when two consecutive ones agree within tolerance, capped at some governor-scale maximum (a few hundred ms).
- The final probe — the one that demonstrated stability — **is the start bracket**. No separate instrument, no double cost; warmup termination and the start-bracket measurement are the same act.
- On a warm box (performance governor, mid-session) it exits almost immediately — near-zero tax. On a deep-idle box it runs as long as the ramp does, which is precisely the adaptive behavior a fixed anything can't give.
- Hitting the cap without stabilizing is itself a gauge signal: "run started unstable" — the machine never settled, and the grade should say so rather than the warmup pretending it did. That converts the failure mode into information instead of a silent bad run.

The costs are two new thresholds (agreement tolerance, cap) — constants of the kind this project has learned to distrust, so they'd want the same loud-fail treatment as the -5 thresholds — and floors-not-means in the probes so one preemption doesn't fake stability or instability. `pick_inner` then runs after stability, which also retroactively firms up the micro-probe's readings. This is now three connected refinements to Todo #1 (time-axis regression, differential brackets, warm-until-stable fused with the start bracket) — worth landing in the entry as a coherent update rather than carrying in conversation. Want me to rewrite Todo #1 to fold them in?

The plain version: today the warmup runs a fixed number of repetitions, so fast operations finish warming in microseconds — long before the CPU has actually sped up to full clock. Better to keep warming until the measurements themselves stop changing, then stop: a warm machine costs almost nothing, a cold machine gets exactly the time it needs, and if it never settles, that fact goes into the run's grade instead of being hidden.

2-in-a-row can indeed be an accident, and you're not wrong — there's even a mechanism-specific reason it's worse than generic noise would suggest. Frequency governors climb through discrete P-states, and a dwell at an intermediate state is exactly two-probes-shaped: readings plateau for a beat, then step again. Two consecutive floors agreeing can certify a ledge on the staircase, not the top. (One-sided noise is the *lesser* risk here — floors are robust against upward contamination; the stepwise ramp is the real spoofer, and it's the very ladder shape 0.22 kept meeting.) Three consecutive agreements require the plateau to outlast two full probe intervals, which most dwells won't; and since each probe is ~1 ms, demanding 3–4 costs single-digit milliseconds on a warm box — trivial insurance. I'd spec it as a small constant defaulting to 3, with 5 as the paranoid end; past that you're buying little and delaying cap-detection of a genuinely unstable box.

message.content: Seems to me that our dynamic warm-up should be part of the pick_inner and we kill two birds with one stone?

content.text:
Yes — and it's better than two-birds convenience; the fusion fixes a subtle defect in the separated design. The strongest version of it: make the warmup probe *be* the sizing probe, repeated until it converges.

The reasoning:

- The quantity `pick_inner` needs (step-cost floor, plus the timer-frame micro-probe) is exactly the quantity whose stability we care about. So "warm until stable" naturally becomes "repeat the sizing probe until K consecutive floors agree, and the final one *is* the sizing input." The convergence test runs on the very number we're about to consume — you can't certify stability on a proxy and then measure the real thing in a different regime, which is a residual risk of a separate warmup.
- It guarantees post-ramp sizing by construction. Today `estimate_step_cost` runs right after the fixed warmup, i.e. potentially mid-ramp — that's the actual bug behind mid-ramp `pick_inner` sizing. Fused, the sizing number can't exist until stability has been demonstrated, so the defect is structurally impossible rather than hopefully avoided.
- The probe load is the *bench's own* steps, so the warmup warms the right things — the bench's code path, caches, branch predictors — and generates the load that drives the governor up, not just timer-read spin.
- Bonus bird: the hard cap on the probe loop is very close to the "deadline the estimate phase" bullet in Todo #3 (the `--pin 8` livelock hang). One capped probe loop can serve both — a bench that never converges *and* a bench that's pathologically slow both hit the same deadline with a diagnostic, instead of hanging.

One thing the fusion quietly changes: the probe now measures step-cost floor at a single N, not an N-sweep — so the "start bracket" doubling loses the slope/intercept decomposition. I think that's fine and arguably cleaner: differential QC becomes "repeat the same probe at run end and compare floors" — same instrument, start vs. end, no acquisition of any second axis. The N-sweep decomposition stays an Ideas-tier option if the batch data ever shows we need to distinguish frame shifts from per-iteration shifts.

I'll fold this into the Todo #2 entry.

message.content: How will it handle situations where inner is small like 1?

content.text:
Short answer: `inner = 1` is the easy case for *sizing* but the awkward case for *probing* — and conveniently, the stakes fall exactly where the probing gets expensive.

Unpacking that:

- **The mechanism doesn't depend on `inner` at all.** The probe loop runs before sizing and measures raw step cost; `pick_inner` returning 1 just means the step is slow enough that framing is negligible. Convergence logic is unchanged. The real variable behind your question is *step cost*, because that's what sets how many steps fit in a probe.
- **Where it bites: a fixed ~1 ms probe starves.** At 25 µs/step (zcr-mpsc territory) a 1 ms probe holds ~40 steps — a floor over 40 is serviceable. At ms-scale steps it holds one or zero, and a "floor" of one sample is just a sample. So the probe must adapt: minimum step count *or* minimum wall time, whichever is larger — meaning probe duration grows with step cost, and K=3 probes of a slow bench can want ~1 s of warmup.
- **That collides with the cap, so the cap's exit must distinguish two causes.** Hitting the deadline because consecutive floors *disagreed* means "run started unstable" — a genuine gauge signal. Hitting it because steps are too slow to complete K adequate probes means "too slow to certify" — proceed, but label the run as uncertified rather than unstable. One deadline, two diagnostics; conflating them would hand slow benches a permanent false F, the r5-7600x mistake in a new costume.
- **Two effects soften the slow-step case.** First, slow probes span more wall time each, so consecutive agreement naturally covers governor timescales — the ramp-detection job partly does itself; the fast benches that need many probes are also the ones whose probes are cheap. Second, the harm being prevented shrinks: mid-ramp sizing error matters when `inner` is large and sensitive, but at `inner = 1` the sizing can't come out wrong (it's the minimum), and framing is noise against a µs-scale step. The residual value of warmup there is warming the bench's own path and giving the start-floor for end-of-run differential QC — worth having, not worth a second of stubborn probing, which argues for the "certify or proceed-with-label" exit rather than blocking.

I'll add that adaptation to the Todo #2 entry.

# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running
artifact. The scheme — the cycle step-numbering and the
unique-per-commit aim — is generic and shared across projects:
this file is copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
covering each medium by conditional rather than per-project
edits.

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version** — the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`),
  written with `-` in prose, ladders, chores, todo, and commit
  talk; its suffix encodes the cycle phase (see
  [Step numbering](#step-numbering)).
- **version-of-record** — the authoritative stored copy of the
  version, in the project's manifest (see
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record));
  a built or running artifact derives from it.
- **versioning** — the topic: this scheme as a whole.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and
surfaced, and how often it changes — pick the case that fits
your medium:

- **Manifest** — where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the
    committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic
    `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, …) — add the case as
    needed
- **Notation** — how the `-` form is stored:
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`),
    store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python
    project), remap to `+` — `0.3.0-5.3.0` → `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same
    version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter** — how a built artifact surfaces the
  version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence** — how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement);
  this project follows the per-commit preference.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change
on **every commit**, so a built or running artifact identifies
the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project
  following the cycle protocol may bump less often — once per
  cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
  if it differs.

  **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA, which a commit cannot
  contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
7	the conversation — code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
8	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
9	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
10	equivalents — this project's manifest is recorded in
11	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
12	
13	## Cycles
14	
15	A cycle has three phases:
16	
17	- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's
18	  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
19	  it and starts at `-1` — see
20	  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
21	  cycle:
22	  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
23	    and the suffix scheme are project-specific — see
24	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
25	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
26	    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
27	    statement + plan ladder).
28	  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
29	- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the
30	  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
31	  needs; each runs through the
32	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
33	- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's
34	  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
35	  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
36	    `## Done`.
37	  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
38	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
39	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
40	    changed.
41	
42	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
43	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
44	result must always be published at close-out. See
45	[Pushing](#pushing).
46	
47	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
48	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`
49	Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
50	Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
51	at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
52	suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
53	for the local-ladder mechanics.
54	
55	## Chores sections
56	
57	A **chores section** is a `##` section in
58	`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
59	general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
60	should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
61	chores file.
62	
63	The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
64	`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
65	with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
66	followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. **Each work commit
67	then appends its own As-built rung + narrative note as it
68	lands** — the chores record is built up per commit, not held
69	back and written all at once at close-out; close-out only
70	*finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
71	`## In Progress` block). The `Commits:` line is backfilled
72	later, once the commit is permanent (see
73	[Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
74	
75	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
76	design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
77	AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).
78	
79	### Commits backfill
80	
81	A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
82	records, by SHA — but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
83	lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
84	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
85	squash rewrites it on the way. So:
86	
87	- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
88	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
89	  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
90	  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
91	  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
92	  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
93	  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands —
94	  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
95	  invalidate.
96	
97	Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one

# Cycle protocol

This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.

The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
the conversation — code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
equivalents — this project's manifest is recorded in
[versioning.md](versioning.md).

## Cycles

A cycle has three phases:

- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's
  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
  it and starts at `-1` — see
  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
  cycle:
  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
    and the suffix scheme are project-specific — see
    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
    statement + plan ladder).
  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …) — the
  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
  needs; each runs through the
  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's
  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
    `## Done`.
  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
    [chores section](#chores-sections).
  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
    changed.

A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
result must always be published at close-out. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
warrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`
Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
for the local-ladder mechanics.

## Chores sections

A **chores section** is a `##` section in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
chores file.

The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. **Each work commit
then appends its own As-built rung + narrative note as it
lands** — the chores record is built up per commit, not held
back and written all at once at close-out; close-out only
*finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
`## In Progress` block). The `Commits:` line is backfilled
later, once the commit is permanent (see
[Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).

### Commits backfill

A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
records, by SHA — but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
squash rewrites it on the way. So:

- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands —
  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
  invalidate.

Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
section records multiple commits (a merge non-ff close-out) —
with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's `# References`
(format in AGENTS.md
[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
`git log --grep "<title>"`.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma — a
**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
SHA must be permanent.

## Preparation

The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
setup (a lightweight cycle omits it — see
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):

  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
  project-specific — see [versioning.md](versioning.md).

vc-x1 0.71.0

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main` — one resumable command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (tracking / bot-published / sync checks —
no build steps; run project checks yourself before pushing)
→ review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-work → commit-bot (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(work repo → <bookmark>, bot repo → main) → push-work →
squash-push-bot. Failures in commit-work / commit-bot /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-work.
After push-work succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version
          Print the `vc-x1 X.Y.Z` banner as the first line, then continue. With
          no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
          
          Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after printing): the
          banner now rides along with normal subcommand execution rather than
          gating it, so scripts can capture the version *and* the command's
          output in one invocation.

      --restart
          Clear any saved state file and start from stage 1

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --from <STAGE>
          Explicit stage to jump to (advanced / debug use)

          Possible values:
          - preflight:       Verify bookmark tracking, the bot-published
            invariant, and sync state
          - review:          Present diff for the first approval gate
          - message:         Compose / edit the commit message; present for
            second gate
          - commit-work:     Commit the work repo
          - commit-bot:      Commit the `.claude` bot repo (skipped if empty)
          - bookmark-set:    Advance each repo's bookmark to its `@-`: work →
            `<bookmark>`, bot → `main`
          - push-work:       `jj git push --bookmark <b> -R .`
          - squash-push-bot: In-process squash of `.claude`'s trailing session
            writes + push `main`

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --status
          Print where the saved state thinks we are and exit

      --recheck
          Re-run `preflight` even on resume (default: skip if last run
          succeeded)

      --no-squash-push
          Stop before `squash-push-bot` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
